1) 유가 급등과 호르무즈 해협 리스크 재부각 (2) 이란의 휴전·해협 재개방 제안이 거부되며 브렌트가 약 107달러, WTI가 약 96달러로 급등(약 +3%대)했고 디젤 등 정제제품 가격도 동반 상승했다. 이는 에너지발 물가 압력을 키워 미 PCE·CPI 등 인플레이션 지표에 상방 리스크를 더하고, 장기물 금리 상승과 달러 강세를 자극하는 요인으로 작용하고 있다. 해협 병목 가능성은 원유·해상운임 프리미엄을 높여 글로벌 위험자산 변동성의 재료가 된다. 2) 미 국채 수익률의 동반 급등과 실질금리 고점 갱신 (2) 10년물은 5%대를 터치하며 다년래 고점, 30년물은 2004년 이후 최고 수준으로 상승했고 2년물도 고점권에 머물며 커브가 더 평탄화됐다. 실질금리도 2008년 이후 고점대로 올라 리스크자산 할인율, 크레딧 스프레드, 밸류에이션에 광범위한 압력을 주는 환경이 조성됐다. 채권 랠리/리스크온과의 상관 구조 변화 여부는 주식·금·달러의 동시 추세에 직결된다. 3) 연준 추가 인상 확률과 이번 주 핵심 지표(미 PCE·고용) 대기 (2) 시장은 10월 25bp 추가 인상 확률을 약 70%로 재가격화했고, 연말까지 누적 약 33bp 긴축 기대가 반영됐다. 이번 주 미국 8월 PCE와 9월 고용보고서가 연준의 “더 오래 높은 금리” 경로를 뒷받침할지 가늠할 포인트로 제시되고 있다. 일부 하우스는 9월 CPI를 ‘스윙 팩터’로 지목하며, 에너지·주거비 세부항목의 모멘텀에 주목하라고 제시한다. 데이터와 연준 발언 톤 변화는 금리·달러·주식 간 연쇄 반응의 촉매가 될 수 있다. 4) 달러 강세와 금가격 급락의 크로스애셋 신호 (2) 미 금리 급등과 긴축 재가격화 속에 달러지수가 강세를 보였고 금은 약 4% 하락했다. 이는 안전자산 내 선호 변화와 글로벌 유동성 여건을 반영하며, 유로화 약세(EUR/USD 1.14 하회)와 함께 역외 달러 조달 비용, 원자재 결제 통화 효과를 통해 EM·원자재 전반으로 파급될 수 있다. 유럽 측에선 라가르드 연설과 유로존 HICP 예비치가 금리·FX 방향성 민감도를 높이고 있다. 5) 중동 지정학 헤드라인 리스크의 상시 변동성 요인화 (2) 호르무즈 해협 관련 제안 거부와 중재 소식이 번갈아 전해지며 주식이 동반 약세를 보였고, 유가·금리 변동성이 확대됐다. 이 이슈는 단기간에도 원유공급 우려→인플레이션 기대→정책금리 경로·장기금리 재가격화로 이어지는 전이 경로를 촉발할 수 있어, 관련 헤드라인의 빈도·강도를 모니터링할 필요가 있다.

Key macro drivers and the BMO outlook: - Near-term headwinds: Higher yields, potential oil-driven inflation, and a hawkish rate environment weigh on gold and silver. - Long-term bullish factors (per BMO Capital Markets): - Substantial re-pricing into a higher long-term base: gold average long-term forecast raised to about $4,000/oz (from $3,100), signaling a structurally higher baseline. - 2026 Q4 near-term view: gold expected around $4,650/oz, with a slight downgrade from prior quarter ($4,750/oz) but still implying a continued price path higher through 2027. - Demand dynamics: Chinese demand is viewed as countercyclical and supportive; subdued yields are not sufficient to derail the long-term uptrend. - The “debasement” and dedollarisation themes are influencing prices more than traditional yield drivers. - Risks skew to the upside unless oil spikes trigger a renewed risk-off or a major jump in rates. Takeaway: - In the near term, gold/silver remain pressured by rising yields and higher oil, but the longer-term macro thesis remains constructive due to monetary debasement, China demand, and dedollarisation trends. BMO’s long-run baseline for gold is now around $4,000/oz, with potential upside toward, or beyond, $5,000/oz depending on inflation dynamics, central bank policy, and geopolitical risk.

Full Report: OECD Economic Outlook, Interim Report September 2026 | OECD

Summary: - The OECD Interim Economic Outlook flags higher risk to agricultural commodity prices from two main factors: (1) elevated energy and fertiliser costs tied to Middle East disruptions, and (2) climate-driven supply shocks, notably a very strong El Niño projected for late 2026. - El Niño is expected to disrupt rainfall and crop conditions in key producing regions (Australia, India, Indonesia, parts of Southeast Asia), potentially boosting prices for farmed commodities in affected areas and increasing global food price pressures for up to two years. - Food price trajectories may be notably higher in 2027 (about 10% above baseline in the scenario with a very strong El Niño), with negative effects on agricultural production in the most exposed Latin American, African, and Asia-Pacific economies. - Fertiliser supply disruptions from Gulf economies and higher energy costs are contributing to higher input costs, feeding into elevated refining margins and consumer prices. - Overall, agricultural prices are sensitive to weather shocks, fertiliser/energy disruptions, and geopolitical developments; upside risks include faster AI-driven productivity gains, while downside risks include sustained supply shocks and higher long-term yields that could reprice asset markets and dampen growth. FAO Cereal Supply and Demand Brief | MTS Insights
www.mtsinsights.com · 2026-10-02T00:00:00.000Z

Summary: - FAO’s 2026 cereal outlook: global production forecast trimmed to 2,980 million tonnes (down 3.4 Mt since July; 2.0% below 2025). Still the second-largest harvest on record. - Maize: world output now 1,309 Mt, down 0.6% from June projections. Declines driven by EU heat/drought (France, Poland) and weaker prospects in India and Paraguay; Argentina and Brazil mirror upside revisions with above-average yields. - Wheat: forecast improved overall, offsetting some downgrades for China, the Philippines, and a larger cut for the USA (lower plantings). - Rice: 2026/27 world production projected at 553.1 Mt (milled), down 1.9% from 2025/26 due to tighter margins and El Niño-adverse weather. - Trade view: world cereal trade in 2026/27 revised up by 0.3% to 509.3 Mt, supported by stronger maize trade and U.S. export leadership; Argentina also raising exports close to Brazil. Black Sea flow uncertainties persist due to shipping/logistics constraints. - Rice trade (2026): raised to 60.5 Mt, driven by Philippines imports, but overall world rice trade still expected to fall ~1.9% from the 2025 peak due to weaker Asian/African import demand. - Barley trade outlook lowered for the EU, Russia, and Ukraine; Australia and Canada remain contributors, especially to China. - Key takeaway: while 2026 cereal production remains robust overall, uneven regional prospects (notably EU maize and some major exporters) and ongoing shipping/logistics risks shape a cautious global market.

Fertiliser affordability pressure despite easing supply risks | Eyre Peninsula Advocate
epadvocate.com.au · 2026-09-25T00:00:00.000Z

Rabobank’s semi-annual global fertiliser outlook says fertiliser affordability remains a key drag on demand through 2027, despite easing supply risks. Key points: - Freight and supply disruptions have eased somewhat, but high fertiliser prices persist, outpacing major agricultural commodity prices. - Farmers are cutting application rates, rotating away from high-nitrogen crops, and shifting to less nitrogen-intensive systems due to costs. - Global phosphate fertilisers face the strongest affordability squeeze due to ongoing supply constraints and high production costs; near-record sulphur prices in H1 2026 pushed up phosphate costs, with expected 7% drop in global phosphate demand in 2026. - Nitrogen markets show gradual improvement: urea prices have eased after peak volatility; expected global urea demand to fall ~5% this year before recovering as affordability improves. - Potash remains the most stable major nutrient; affordability weakened slightly but supply less affected by geopolitical disruption, with relatively stable demand vs 2025. - For Australia, monitor global grain/oilseed markets; world crop inventories remain historically high, providing some buffer against shocks, though stocks are forecast to dip slightly for 2026 (wheat, corn, rice). - Main near-term risks: El Niño impacts on crop production, rising farm input costs, and ongoing Black Sea export challenges; these could push commodity prices higher toward recent upper ranges. Overall: The agricultural commodities market faces a mixed outlook—improving nitrogen affordability and imports risk relief amid stubborn phosphate costs and high overall fertiliser prices, with demand constrained by costs and weather, and upside risk from El Niño and export disruptions.

Food exports through 2035: India, Southeast Asia and MENA amid rising demand and growing imports - Italian Food News
Redazione IFN · 2026-09-22T00:00:00.000Z

Summary: The OECD-FAO Agricultural Outlook 2026-2035 projects a shift in global agricultural demand and trade, with growth concentrated in low- and middle-income countries. India and Southeast Asia are set to drive consumption growth, while other regions increasingly rely on imports. By 2035, imports could cover about 72% of caloric consumption for the covered agricultural commodities, and regional net imports in the Middle East and North Africa are projected to rise by ~34% over the decade due to population growth and limited domestic production. Global agricultural trade share of production remains around 22-23%, but surpluses and import needs will move geographically. Key implications for producers, importers, and distributors: (1) demand growth may not align with import reliance—domestic production can meet part of rising demand, (2) high import dependence brings exposure to exchange rates, weather shocks, and policy changes, and (3) securing diversified, reliable supply chains and maintaining logistics continuity will be crucial. The Outlook is a baseline scenario, focusing on main commodities and fish, and is not a detailed forecast for processed foods.

A relocation of surplus to China previously supported a London squeeze; since late August, liquidity flows are normalizing as inventories and backwardation recede. Cash-to-three-month backwardation narrowed from about $232 to ~$87 (Aug 27 to Sept 21), signaling easing immediate tightness. - Supply dislocations persist, but constraints deepen: ILZSG notes world mine production down ~2.6% in H1, with concentrate treatment charges deeply negative, indicating material bottlenecks at the mine-to-feed stage. Smelter terms have deteriorated (negative Zn50 treatment charges in China), transferring bargaining power to miners and keeping concentrate tight. - Near-term price path (base case): Backwardation normalizes as Chinese export flows persist, while the zinc flat price remains elevated due to ongoing mine-supply losses and negative treatment charges. Chinese visible inventories continue to draw without strong evidence of downstream demand acceleration. This supports a price remains high relative to fundamentals, but with a risk of volatility tied to concentrate availability. - Upside risks: If concentrate scarcity translates into weaker refined production in Q4, China’s metal available for export may tighten, reinforcing the price and potential London backwardation widening again. - Downside risks: If the export arbitrage stays open longer than anticipated and more metal arrives, or if a broader rebuild of London deliverable stocks occurs, price pressure could ease and the backwardation tightens further toward normal levels. - Market-sensitive indicators to watch: - Concentrate treatment charges: further deterioration vs improvement. - Chinese visible inventories and export flows: sustained draw vs stabilization. - Smelter input terms and refined production: any pause or acceleration. - Fund positioning: growing shorts in LME metals could cap upside or amplify downside moves. - Implications for copper and aluminum (macro context): While the report centers on zinc, the macro picture suggests higher attention to base metal supply tightness and downstream demand in 4Q24. For copper and aluminum: - Copper: potential sensitivity to refined supply constraints and China demand signals; monitor inventories, treatment charges in related supply chains, and LME positioning. - Aluminum: downstream demand and energy-linked production costs remain crucial; watch the balance of supply disruptions and user inventory cycles. Bottom line: Zinc remains under supply-driven pressure with a risk-reward skew toward continued elevated pricing if concentrate scarcity persists into Q4, but a moderation in backwardation and inventories could ease near term if Chinese exports remain robust and concentrate availability improves. For copper and aluminum, macro risk hinges on broader demand signals and upstream supply tightness; the zinc dynamics imply a cautious stance on all base metals—watch treatment charges, inventories, and export flows as key macro catalysts.
